## ✏️ Paper 7 [6584]-91 — Question 17 of 19

**📄 Paper:** [6584]-91
**🔢 Original Question:** Q7(b)
**⭐ Marks:** 8 marks

---

### ❓ Full Question

Compare and contrast **row-wise** and **block-wise** approaches in multithreaded matrix multiplication with respect to:
- Division of work
- Communication overhead
- Cache efficiency

---

### 📌 What is this question about?

When parallelizing matrix multiplication, we can divide the work between threads in different ways. Two common strategies are **row-wise** (each thread handles complete rows of the result) and **block-wise** (each thread handles a rectangular block of the result). This question compares these two strategies.

**Real-world analogy:** Painting a wall with multiple painters:
- **Row-wise:** Each painter paints complete horizontal strips
- **Block-wise:** Each painter paints a rectangular section

---

### 🔢 Solution

### PART 1 — INTRODUCTION

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  CONTEXT: Multiplying A(m×n) × B(n×p) = C(m×p)        │
│                                                         │
│  Each element C[i][j] requires n multiplications       │
│  and n-1 additions (inner product of row i of A        │
│  with column j of B).                                  │
│                                                         │
│  QUESTION: How do we DIVIDE this work among threads?   │
│                                                         │
│  TWO STRATEGIES:                                        │
│  1. ROW-WISE: Thread t handles all columns of row t    │
│  2. BLOCK-WISE: Thread t handles a rectangular block   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

---

### PART 2 — ROW-WISE APPROACH

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  ROW-WISE APPROACH                                      │
│                                                         │
│  DESCRIPTION:                                           │
│  → Divide result matrix C into m rows                  │
│  → Thread i computes ALL elements of ROW i of C       │
│  → Each thread handles p elements (one full row)      │
│                                                         │
│  VISUALIZATION (C is 4×4, 4 threads):                  │
│  Thread 0: [C[0][0], C[0][1], C[0][2], C[0][3]]      │
│  Thread 1: [C[1][0], C[1][1], C[1][2], C[1][3]]      │
│  Thread 2: [C[2][0], C[2][1], C[2][2], C[2][3]]      │
│  Thread 3: [C[3][0], C[3][1], C[3][2], C[3][3]]      │
│                                                         │
│  Each thread reads: ENTIRE row of A (A[i][0..n-1])   │
│                     ENTIRE matrix B (all columns)      │
│                                                         │
│  pseudocode:                                            │
│  parallel for i = 0 to m-1:     ← Each thread one row │
│    for j = 0 to p-1:            ← Sequential          │
│      C[i][j] = dot_product(A[i], B[:,j])               │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

---

### PART 3 — BLOCK-WISE APPROACH

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  BLOCK-WISE APPROACH                                    │
│                                                         │
│  DESCRIPTION:                                           │
│  → Divide result matrix C into rectangular BLOCKS      │
│  → Thread (i,j) computes a BLOCK of C                 │
│  → Block size = (m/√P) × (p/√P) for P threads        │
│                                                         │
│  VISUALIZATION (C is 4×4, 4 threads/blocks):           │
│  [Thread0 | Thread1]                                   │
│  [Thread2 | Thread3]                                   │
│                                                         │
│  Thread 0: C[0..1][0..1]  ← top-left block            │
│  Thread 1: C[0..1][2..3]  ← top-right block           │
│  Thread 2: C[2..3][0..1]  ← bottom-left block         │
│  Thread 3: C[2..3][2..3]  ← bottom-right block        │
│                                                         │
│  Each thread reads: BLOCK of rows of A               │
│                     BLOCK of columns of B             │
│                                                         │
│  pseudocode:                                            │
│  parallel for ib = 0 to m/B-1:   ← Block rows        │
│    parallel for jb = 0 to p/B-1: ← Block columns     │
│      compute block C[ib*B..(ib+1)*B][jb*B..(jb+1)*B] │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

---

### PART 4 — COMPARISON TABLE

```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  COMPARISON: ROW-WISE vs BLOCK-WISE                          │
│                                                              │
│  1. DIVISION OF WORK                                         │
│  ────────────────────                                         │
│  Row-wise:                                                   │
│  → Divide by ROWS only (1D decomposition)                   │
│  → P threads → m rows → m/P rows per thread                 │
│  → Work per thread = (m/P) × p × n operations               │
│  → Simple, straightforward division                         │
│  → Works best when m is large (many rows)                  │
│                                                              │
│  Block-wise:                                                 │
│  → Divide by ROWS AND COLUMNS (2D decomposition)            │
│  → P threads → √P × √P blocks                              │
│  → Work per thread = (m/√P) × (p/√P) × n operations        │
│  → More complex but more granular control                   │
│  → Works well even when m is small                          │
│                                                              │
│  WINNER for load balance: Block-wise (more granular)        │
│                                                              │
│  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  │
│  2. COMMUNICATION OVERHEAD                                   │
│  ──────────────────────────                                  │
│  Row-wise:                                                   │
│  → Thread i needs: Row i of A + ALL of B                   │
│  → ALL threads read ENTIRE matrix B                         │
│  → High memory bandwidth for B (same data read P times)    │
│  → Communication ∝ O(m×n/P + n×p) per thread               │
│                                                              │
│  Block-wise:                                                 │
│  → Thread (i,j) needs: Block of rows of A + Block of B    │
│  → Each thread reads SUBSET of B (not all of B)            │
│  → Lower total data movement across all threads            │
│  → Communication ∝ O(m×n/√P + n×p/√P) per thread          │
│                                                              │
│  WINNER for communication: Block-wise (less data moved)     │
│                                                              │
│  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  │
│  3. CACHE EFFICIENCY                                         │
│  ──────────────────────                                      │
│  Row-wise:                                                   │
│  → Thread reads row of A: contiguous in memory → GOOD cache│
│  → Thread reads columns of B: B stored row-major in C/C++   │
│    → Column access is STRIDED (non-contiguous) → POOR cache │
│  → Many cache misses when accessing columns of B            │
│  → Cache efficiency: MODERATE                               │
│                                                              │
│  Block-wise:                                                 │
│  → Thread's block of A: rows are contiguous → GOOD         │
│  → Thread's block of B: if B is pre-transposed or block-   │
│    stored → GOOD cache usage                                │
│  → Blocks fit in cache better → FEWER cache misses         │
│  → High data REUSE within each block computation           │
│  → Cache efficiency: HIGH                                   │
│                                                              │
│  WINNER for cache efficiency: Block-wise                    │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

---

### PART 5 — SUMMARY TABLE

```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Feature            │ Row-Wise         │ Block-Wise          │
│  ───────────────────┼──────────────────┼─────────────────── │
│  Decomposition      │ 1D (rows only)   │ 2D (rows+columns)  │
│  Division of work   │ Simple, m rows   │ Complex, √P×√P     │
│  Load balance       │ Good if m>>P     │ Better (granular)  │
│  Communication      │ HIGH (all read B)│ LOWER (subset of B)│
│  Cache efficiency   │ Moderate         │ HIGH               │
│  B matrix access    │ Entire B per thd │ Partial B per thd  │
│  Implementation     │ SIMPLER ✓        │ More complex       │
│  Best when          │ Few threads      │ Many threads       │
│  Scalability        │ Limited by m     │ Better scalability  │
│  Overall winner     │ Simple cases     │ Large-scale ★      │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

---

### ✅ Final Answer

```
╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
║  FINAL ANSWER:                                           ║
║                                                          ║
║  1. DIVISION OF WORK:                                    ║
║  Row-wise: 1D decomposition, simple m/P rows per thread ║
║  Block-wise: 2D decomposition, √P×√P blocks, granular  ║
║  Winner: Block-wise (better load balance)               ║
║                                                          ║
║  2. COMMUNICATION OVERHEAD:                              ║
║  Row-wise: Each thread reads ENTIRE matrix B → HIGH     ║
║  Block-wise: Each thread reads PARTIAL B → LOWER        ║
║  Winner: Block-wise (less data movement)                ║
║                                                          ║
║  3. CACHE EFFICIENCY:                                    ║
║  Row-wise: Strided column access of B → POOR cache      ║
║  Block-wise: Block data reuse → HIGH cache efficiency   ║
║  Winner: Block-wise (fewer cache misses)                ║
║                                                          ║
║  Overall: Block-wise is superior for large-scale       ║
║  parallel matrix multiplication.                        ║
╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝
```

---

Address all three comparison aspects (**work, communication, cache**) separately. Use a **comparison table** — examiners love this structure. State the **winner** for each aspect. Explain WHY block-wise has better cache efficiency (block data reuse vs strided column access).

## ✏️ Paper 7 [6584]-91 — Question 18 of 19

**📄 Paper:** [6584]-91
**🔢 Original Question:** Q8(a)
**⭐ Marks:** 10 marks

---

### ❓ Full Question

Consider the text T and the pattern text P. Write a **naïve string-matching** algorithm. Show the stepwise process of working of this algorithm if:

> **T = "KITCHEN"** and **P = "HEN"**

---

### 📌 What is this question about?

The **Naïve (Brute Force) String Matching** algorithm checks every possible position in text T to see if pattern P starts there. It's the simplest approach — no preprocessing, no clever tricks, just check every position character by character.

**Real-world analogy:** Finding the word "HEN" in a sentence by placing your finger under the first letter, comparing 3 characters, then moving one position right and repeating — until you find the match or reach the end.

---

### 🔢 Step-by-Step Solution

#### STEP 1 — Setup

```
Text T    = "KITCHEN"     (n = 7)
Pattern P = "HEN"         (m = 3)

T indices: K=1, I=2, T=3, C=4, H=5, E=6, N=7
P indices: H=1, E=2, N=3

Number of positions to try: n - m + 1 = 7 - 3 + 1 = 5
Positions s = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4  (0-indexed)
```

---

#### STEP 2 — Naïve String Matching Algorithm

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  ALGORITHM: Naïve-String-Matcher(T, P)                  │
│                                                         │
│  n = length(T)       // = 7 for "KITCHEN"              │
│  m = length(P)       // = 3 for "HEN"                  │
│                                                         │
│  for s = 0 to (n - m) do     // s = shift position    │
│  {                                                      │
│    j = 1                      // Start from P[1]       │
│    match = TRUE                                         │
│                                                         │
│    while j ≤ m AND match do   // Compare m characters  │
│    {                                                    │
│      if T[s + j] ≠ P[j] then  // Character mismatch   │
│        match = FALSE           // Stop comparing        │
│      else                                               │
│        j = j + 1              // Move to next char     │
│    }                                                    │
│                                                         │
│    if match == TRUE then                               │
│      print "Pattern found at position", s + 1          │
│  }                                                      │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

---

#### STEP 3 — Stepwise Trace

**Text: K I T C H E N**
**Index: 1 2 3 4 5 6 7**
**Pattern: H E N**

---

**Shift s=0: Compare P with T[1..3] = "KIT"**

```
Alignment:
T: K  I  T  C  H  E  N
P: H  E  N
   ↑

Compare P[1]='H' with T[1]='K':
  'H' ≠ 'K' → MISMATCH ✗
  Stop comparing (no need to check P[2], P[3])

Result: NO MATCH at position 1
```

---

**Shift s=1: Compare P with T[2..4] = "ITC"**

```
Alignment:
T: K  I  T  C  H  E  N
      P: H  E  N
         ↑

Compare P[1]='H' with T[2]='I':
  'H' ≠ 'I' → MISMATCH ✗
  Stop comparing immediately.

Result: NO MATCH at position 2
```

---

**Shift s=2: Compare P with T[3..5] = "TCH"**

```
Alignment:
T: K  I  T  C  H  E  N
         P: H  E  N
            ↑

Compare P[1]='H' with T[3]='T':
  'H' ≠ 'T' → MISMATCH ✗
  Stop comparing immediately.

Result: NO MATCH at position 3
```

---

**Shift s=3: Compare P with T[4..6] = "CHE"**

```
Alignment:
T: K  I  T  C  H  E  N
            P: H  E  N
               ↑

Compare P[1]='H' with T[4]='C':
  'H' ≠ 'C' → MISMATCH ✗
  Stop comparing immediately.

Result: NO MATCH at position 4
```

---

**Shift s=4: Compare P with T[5..7] = "HEN"**

```
Alignment:
T: K  I  T  C  H  E  N
               P: H  E  N
                  ↑

Compare P[1]='H' with T[5]='H':
  'H' = 'H' → MATCH ✓ Continue...

Compare P[2]='E' with T[6]='E':
  'E' = 'E' → MATCH ✓ Continue...

Compare P[3]='N' with T[7]='N':
  'N' = 'N' → MATCH ✓ All m=3 characters matched!

match = TRUE → Pattern found!

Result: MATCH FOUND at position 5 (s+1 = 4+1 = 5) ★
```

---

#### STEP 4 — Visual Summary of All Shifts

```
T: K  I  T  C  H  E  N
   1  2  3  4  5  6  7

s=0: H  E  N                    → K≠H ✗
     ^
s=1:    H  E  N                 → I≠H ✗
        ^
s=2:       H  E  N              → T≠H ✗
           ^
s=3:          H  E  N           → C≠H ✗
              ^
s=4:             H  E  N        → H=H✓ E=E✓ N=N✓ ★ MATCH at position 5!
                 ^  ^  ^
                 ALL 3 MATCH!
```

---

#### STEP 5 — Comparison Table

| Shift s | Window T | P[1] vs T[s+1] | P[2] vs T[s+2] | P[3] vs T[s+3] | Result |
|---------|----------|----------------|----------------|----------------|--------|
| 0 | "KIT" | H≠K ✗ | — | — | No match |
| 1 | "ITC" | H≠I ✗ | — | — | No match |
| 2 | "TCH" | H≠T ✗ | — | — | No match |
| 3 | "CHE" | H≠C ✗ | — | — | No match |
| 4 | "HEN" | H=H ✓ | E=E ✓ | N=N ✓ | **MATCH ★** |

**Total comparisons made: 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 3 = 7**

---

### PART 2 — TIME COMPLEXITY ANALYSIS

```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  NAÏVE STRING MATCHING — COMPLEXITY                      │
│                                                          │
│  OUTER LOOP: Runs (n - m + 1) times                     │
│  INNER LOOP: Up to m comparisons per shift              │
│                                                          │
│  WORST CASE:                                             │
│  → Every position requires full m comparisons           │
│  → Example: T = "AAAAAAA", P = "AAAB"                   │
│    At EVERY position, compare m-1 A's before finding B  │
│  → Total: O((n-m+1) × m) ≈ O(nm)                       │
│                                                          │
│  BEST CASE:                                              │
│  → First character never matches                        │
│  → Example: T = "BBBBBBB", P = "AAAB"                   │
│  → Total: O(n-m+1) = O(n)                              │
│                                                          │
│  AVERAGE CASE:                                           │
│  → For random text/pattern: O(n)                        │
│  → Most mismatches occur at first character            │
│                                                          │
│  SPACE COMPLEXITY: O(1)                                  │
│  → No extra arrays needed                               │
│  → Just variables s and j                               │
│                                                          │
│  This example:                                           │
│  n=7, m=3, comparisons = 4×1 + 3 = 7 (best possible)   │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

---

### ✅ Final Answer

```
╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
║  FINAL ANSWER:                                           ║
║                                                          ║
║  Naïve Algorithm: Try pattern at every shift s=0 to n-m ║
║  Compare P[j] with T[s+j] for j=1 to m                 ║
║  If all m match → Pattern found at position s+1         ║
║                                                          ║
║  TRACE for T="KITCHEN", P="HEN":                        ║
║  s=0: K≠H → No match                                   ║
║  s=1: I≠H → No match                                   ║
║  s=2: T≠H → No match                                   ║
║  s=3: C≠H → No match                                   ║
║  s=4: H=H, E=E, N=N → MATCH FOUND at position 5 ★     ║
║                                                          ║
║  TIME COMPLEXITY:                                        ║
║  Best case:  O(n)                                       ║
║  Worst case: O(nm)                                      ║
║  Space:      O(1)                                       ║
╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝
```

## ✏️ Paper 7 [6584]-91 — Question 19 of 19

**📄 Paper:** [6584]-91
**🔢 Original Question:** Q8(b)
**⭐ Marks:** 8 marks

---

### ❓ Full Question

Write a **distributed algorithm to find the minimum spanning tree**.

---

### 📌 What is this question about?

The **Distributed Minimum Spanning Tree (MST)** algorithm runs on multiple computers (processes), where each computer only knows its own edges. They must collectively find the MST through message passing — no single computer sees the whole graph.

**Real-world analogy:** City mayors trying to build the cheapest network of roads. Each mayor only knows the costs to NEIGHBORING cities. They must send letters to each other to coordinate and find the cheapest overall road network.

---

### 🔢 Solution

### PART 1 — BACKGROUND AND MOTIVATION

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  WHY DISTRIBUTED MST?                                   │
│                                                         │
│  SEQUENTIAL MST (Kruskal/Prim):                        │
│  → Runs on ONE computer                               │
│  → Needs ENTIRE graph in memory                        │
│  → O(E log V) time                                    │
│                                                         │
│  DISTRIBUTED MST (GHS Algorithm):                      │
│  → Runs on MULTIPLE computers (processes)              │
│  → Each process = one vertex                          │
│  → Processes communicate via MESSAGES                 │
│  → No single process sees entire graph                │
│  → Designed for large networks (internet scale)       │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

---

### PART 2 — ALGORITHM BASIS: BLUE RULE (KEY INSIGHT)

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  BLUE RULE (Foundation of Distributed MST):            │
│                                                         │
│  For ANY partition of vertices into two groups S and   │
│  (V-S), the MINIMUM WEIGHT EDGE crossing the cut       │
│  (connecting S to V-S) MUST be in the MST.            │
│                                                         │
│  This rule holds because:                              │
│  → If we include a heavier crossing edge instead,     │
│    we could always swap it with the minimum crossing  │
│    edge and get a cheaper spanning tree.              │
│                                                         │
│  DISTRIBUTED USE:                                       │
│  → Each "fragment" (group of vertices) acts as S     │
│  → It finds its Minimum Outgoing Edge (MOE) to       │
│    another fragment                                   │
│  → That MOE must be in the MST!                      │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

---

### PART 3 — COMPLETE DISTRIBUTED MST ALGORITHM (GHS)

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  ALGORITHM: Distributed-MST (Gallager-Humblet-Spira)   │
│                                                         │
│  INITIALIZATION:                                        │
│  → Each vertex vᵢ becomes a FRAGMENT by itself        │
│  → n fragments total at start                         │
│  → Each fragment has a unique FRAGMENT NAME (ID)      │
│  → Each fragment has a LEVEL = 0                      │
│  → Each vertex knows weights of its own edges only    │
│                                                         │
│  DATA MAINTAINED BY EACH VERTEX:                        │
│  → fragment_name: identity of current fragment        │
│  → fragment_level: current level (log n max)          │
│  → MST_edges: edges selected for MST so far           │
│  → edge_states[]: BASIC, BRANCH, or REJECTED          │
│    BASIC = unknown status                             │
│    BRANCH = part of MST                              │
│    REJECTED = not part of MST (within fragment)      │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  MAIN ALGORITHM PHASES (repeat until 1 fragment):      │
│                                                         │
│  PHASE 1: FIND MINIMUM OUTGOING EDGE (MOE)             │
│  ──────────────────────────────────────────              │
│  a. Fragment LEADER sends INITIATE message to all      │
│     vertices in its fragment.                          │
│                                                         │
│  b. Each vertex vᵢ searches for MOE:                   │
│     → Examines all its BASIC edges                    │
│     → For each basic edge (vᵢ, vⱼ):                   │
│       Send TEST message to vⱼ with own fragment name  │
│       If vⱼ replies "ACCEPT":                         │
│         → Edge crosses to different fragment          │
│         → Record as candidate MOE                     │
│       If vⱼ replies "REJECT":                         │
│         → Same fragment → mark edge as REJECTED       │
│     → Report minimum candidate MOE to leader          │
│                                                         │
│  c. Fragment leader COLLECTS all candidate MOEs        │
│     → Picks the GLOBALLY minimum one                  │
│     → This is the fragment's MOE                      │
│                                                         │
│  PHASE 2: MERGE FRAGMENTS                               │
│  ──────────────────────────                              │
│  a. Leader sends CHANGEROOT message routing through   │
│     MST edges to the vertex at one end of MOE.        │
│                                                         │
│  b. That vertex sends CONNECT message on the MOE edge  │
│     to the neighboring fragment.                       │
│                                                         │
│  c. If BOTH fragments want to merge via same edge:     │
│     → ABSORPTION: smaller level merges into larger    │
│     → COMBINE: equal level fragments merge and        │
│       level increases by 1                            │
│                                                         │
│  d. The MOE edge is added to MST_edges ✓              │
│                                                         │
│  PHASE 3: ELECT NEW LEADER                              │
│  ──────────────────────────                              │
│  a. New merged fragment elects a leader                │
│     → Often the vertex with minimum ID in fragment    │
│     → Or the vertex at the new MOE endpoint           │
│                                                         │
│  b. New leader broadcasts new fragment name and level  │
│                                                         │
│  TERMINATION:                                           │
│  → When a fragment's MOE search finds NO outgoing     │
│    edge → this fragment spans the entire graph        │
│  → MST is complete — contains n-1 edges               │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

---

### PART 4 — MESSAGE TYPES

```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  MESSAGE TYPES IN DISTRIBUTED MST:                       │
│                                                          │
│  Message      │ Sender           │ Purpose              │
│  ─────────────┼──────────────────┼─────────────────── │
│  INITIATE     │ Fragment leader  │ Start MOE search in  │
│               │                  │ this fragment        │
│  TEST         │ Any vertex       │ "Are you in a        │
│               │                  │ different fragment?" │
│  ACCEPT       │ Receiver of TEST │ "Yes, different      │
│               │                  │ fragment → MOE!"    │
│  REJECT       │ Receiver of TEST │ "No, same fragment  │
│               │                  │ → not an outgoing   │
│               │                  │ edge"               │
│  REPORT       │ Vertex/subtree   │ "My best MOE is w"  │
│               │                  │ (sends to leader)   │
│  CHANGEROOT   │ Fragment leader  │ Route CONNECT msg to │
│               │                  │ MOE endpoint        │
│  CONNECT      │ MOE endpoint     │ "Merge with me via  │
│               │                  │ this edge"          │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

---

### PART 5 — EXAMPLE TRACE

```
Example graph (4 vertices):
  A --3-- B --2-- C --4-- D
          |               |
          +-------6-------+

Initial fragments: {A}, {B}, {C}, {D}

Round 1:
  Fragment {A}: MOE = A-B (weight 3)
  Fragment {B}: MOE = B-C (weight 2)
  Fragment {C}: MOE = B-C (weight 2) ← same edge!
  Fragment {D}: MOE = C-D (weight 4)

  Merges:
  → B and C merge via edge B-C (weight 2) → fragment {B,C}
     Edge B-C added to MST ✓
  → A merges with {B,C} via edge A-B (weight 3) → {A,B,C}
     Edge A-B added to MST ✓
  → D merges with {A,B,C} via edge C-D (weight 4) → {A,B,C,D}
     Edge C-D added to MST ✓

MST edges: {B-C(2), A-B(3), C-D(4)}
MST weight: 2 + 3 + 4 = 9

(Edge B-D with weight 6 is NOT in MST ✓)
```

---

### PART 6 — COMPLEXITY ANALYSIS

```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  DISTRIBUTED MST COMPLEXITY                              │
│                                                          │
│  NUMBER OF PHASES:                                       │
│  → Fragments at least double each phase                 │
│  → n → n/2 → n/4 → ... → 1                            │
│  → Maximum O(log n) phases                              │
│                                                          │
│  MESSAGES PER PHASE:                                     │
│  → Each edge generates O(1) TEST/REJECT/ACCEPT messages │
│  → Total edges = E → O(E) messages per phase            │
│  → Plus O(n) INITIATE/REPORT/CHANGEROOT messages       │
│  → Total per phase: O(n + E)                           │
│                                                          │
│  TOTAL MESSAGE COMPLEXITY:                               │
│  O((n + E) × log n)                                     │
│                                                          │
│  TIME COMPLEXITY (rounds):                               │
│  O(n × log n) communication rounds                      │
│  (assuming unit message delay)                          │
│                                                          │
│  COMPARISON WITH SEQUENTIAL:                             │
│  → Sequential Kruskal: O(E log E) on 1 computer        │
│  → Distributed GHS: O((n+E) log n) messages total      │
│  → Distributed advantage: handles graphs too large      │
│    for single machine memory                            │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### ✅ Final Answer

```
╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
║  FINAL ANSWER:                                           ║
║                                                          ║
║  DISTRIBUTED MST (GHS Algorithm):                        ║
║                                                          ║
║  Initialization: Each vertex = one fragment (level 0)   ║
║                                                          ║
║  Each Phase (repeat until 1 fragment):                   ║
║  Phase 1 — Find MOE:                                    ║
║    Leader sends INITIATE → vertices send TEST messages  ║
║    Neighbors reply ACCEPT (diff. fragment) or REJECT    ║
║    Minimum weight accepted edge = fragment's MOE        ║
║    Vertices REPORT MOE to leader                        ║
║                                                          ║
║  Phase 2 — Merge:                                       ║
║    Leader sends CHANGEROOT → vertex sends CONNECT on MOE║
║    Two fragments merge → MOE added to MST ✓            ║
║                                                          ║
║  Phase 3 — New leader elected for merged fragment       ║
║                                                          ║
║  Terminates when 1 fragment remains (n-1 MST edges)    ║
║                                                          ║
║  Complexity: O(log n) phases, O((n+E)log n) messages   ║
╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝
```
